content: 1. Information and advice provided to women can sometimes undermine their confidence and lead to frustration. Both healthcare professionals and mothers have reported issues related to conflicting information. 2. Some women believe that lay community counselors can provide breastfeeding support as effectively as, or even better than, healthcare workers. This perception was noted in a study with moderate methodological limitations and limited relevance to the USA. 3. Women have expressed appreciation for breastfeeding peer counselors who are knowledgeable, experienced, responsive to distress calls, and provide support in a personal and caring manner. This was observed in a study with moderate methodological limitations and limited relevance to the USA. 4. Midwives who assisted women during childbirth were reported to have both positive and negative impacts on the mothers' ability to continue breastfeeding. This was highlighted in a study with minor methodological limitations and limited relevance, focusing on low-income countries and HIV populations. 5. Mothers living with HIV and their counselors often had differing views on counseling sessions. Mothers desired counseling, while counselors focused on providing information. This was noted in a study with moderate methodological limitations and relevance to HIV populations in three African countries. 6. Mothers in low-income settings reported very few positive postpartum interactions with medical professionals. This finding was consistent across studies, mostly conducted in high-income countries, with varying methodological limitations. 7. Peer supporters have reported that their work is hindered by a lack of visibility of their roles and a lack of clear identity compared to professional healthcare workers. This was observed in studies conducted in high-income countries. 8. Medical staff acknowledged that women living with HIV often receive or perceive mixed messages from different clinics and staff. Both healthcare professionals and mothers have described issues with conflicting information. 9. Several midwives recognized that mothers need reassurance when starting breastfeeding. They spent time explaining the process and setting expectations to help mothers feel more confident. 10. Participants described challenges in the continuity of care, noting that mothers often see multiple midwives during their hospital stay and encounter different midwives and nurses after discharge. 11. Some healthcare staff reported difficulty in promoting or supporting breastfeeding if they lacked personal experience with it, which made them feel uncomfortable discussing the topic with mothers. 12. Across various disciplines, a lack of time and skills was a common concern, except among lactation counselors, who reported having adequate skills but insufficient time to provide support. 13. Lactation counselors viewed themselves as breastfeeding experts and wished for other providers to adopt a similar approach. They believed their role was more holistic, focusing on empowering women and providing emotional support. 14. Many women lacked extended family nearby and had little experience with babies, which left them with limited practical knowledge about breastfeeding. 15. Women living with HIV and their counselors often had differing expectations of counseling sessions. Mothers sought emotional support and guidance, while counselors prioritized providing information. 16. HIV counselors expressed stress and frustration when mothers did not follow instructions, as this could endanger their children’s lives. Counselors worried that such outcomes might be blamed on them. 17. The advice given to women living with HIV by healthcare workers was sometimes inconsistent with WHO and national recommendations, or at least perceived as such by the mothers. 18. Providers working with women of lower socioeconomic status found it challenging to distinguish between social factors and obesity as causes of poor breastfeeding outcomes. 19. Electronic prompts encouraged providers to discuss the benefits of breastfeeding in greater detail during consultations. 20. It was determined that support workers did not necessarily need expertise in breastfeeding, as their role was considered a lay position. 21. Some women reported feeling unprepared for the realities of breastfeeding, such as discomfort, the time commitment, and common feeding problems. They expressed a desire for more information before their baby was born. 22. Obese patients required more time and attention from providers, which influenced how providers perceived these patients. 23. Physical challenges related to breastfeeding mechanics or general obesity were frequently discussed by healthcare workers. 24. Nurses and lactation consultants suggested that prenatal breast examinations could help identify and address issues like flat nipples before delivery.
